{"id": "8:24/q24", "question": "How does this command connect with the surrounding verses and sura?", "turns_on": "Whether the local sequence stresses renewed obedience, the risk of hearts closing, or the reach of communal accountability.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q24/p1", "position": "It renews the earlier call to obey and warns believers against sharing the fate of those who refused.", "reasons": "Biqa'i links the punishment of unresponsive disbelievers to the warning and 8:22; Ibn Ashur sees a restatement of 8:20 after Badr and 8:1, 8:15 and 8:17. Tabataba'i calls it reinforcement of 8:20; Islahi places 20-28 in believers' gradual reform."}, {"id": "8:24/q24/p2", "position": "The intervention warning follows 8:23: unlike the deaf, believers have a chance to answer before it closes.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya warns disobedience could bring the separation of 8:23. Alusi reports this reconciliation but notes a moral-responsibility difficulty. Biqa'i says the life-giving call counters the deafness, muteness and unreason of 8:22."}, {"id": "8:24/q24/p3", "position": "The life promised here links present obedience to life in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya states the connection; Razi cites 16:97 and 29:64; Tabataba'i describes higher life unveiled beyond worldly play."}, {"id": "8:24/q24/p4", "position": "The following communal warning means unchecked wrongdoing can harm everyone.", "reasons": "Islahi says the whole community must prevent mischief lest the harm engulf it; this belongs to the sequence through 8:28."}]}
{"id": "8:24/q25", "question": "What cautions about Quranic expression and interpretation accompany readings of this verse?", "turns_on": "Different cited cautions concern syntax, meter, figurative language, and the practice of commentary.", "positions": [{"id": "8:24/q25/p1", "position": "Grammatical relations, rather than mere word placement, determine the composed meaning.", "reasons": "Sibawayh's examples distinguish an appositive الرجل with هذا from circumstantial منطلقا and say a pronoun is not modified by an overt noun. Jurjani rejects the silk-weaving analogy and uses Abu Tammam's ink and venom image to show that changing the parse changes the image without moving words. He urges clarity and fidelity to knowledge; he describes eloquence as ranked composition culminating in inimitability."}, {"id": "8:24/q25/p2", "position": "Interpretation should preserve earlier insight while adding grounded understanding.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur describes the Quran as protected guidance and lasting miracle, the Companions' clarification, and his aim to explain law and moral insights, judge between schools, and refine earlier work after hesitation about the burden. Bint al-Shati reports Jurjani's warning against unqualified speculation, his loyalty to knowledge, and his case for Quranic composition's eloquence."}, {"id": "8:24/q25/p3", "position": "Incidental rhythm does not make Quranic speech poetry.", "reasons": "Baqillani says poetry requires intention; a chance rajaz line is insufficient, some demand four rhyming lines, and Quranic fragments vary in rhyme. Arabic meter also requires matched length and syllable pattern; if the Quran were familiar poetry, poets could have imitated it."}, {"id": "8:24/q25/p4", "position": "Images and word choices carry their contextual force, rather than being only rhyme fillers.", "reasons": "Jurjani discusses a thick-lipped black camel image, claws gripping prey as a figure for domination, and Hutay'a's neglected guest. He reports the 'hoof for foot' rhyme explanation but argues the hoof may also evoke a guest's rough journey and forceful driving."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q01", "question": "How does the opening 'when' connect grammatically to the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "Its governor may be an understood command, an earlier time or verb, the Criterion, or God's power.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q01/p1", "position": "It is appositive to the Day of Criterion or the day the armies met.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Ibn Ashur and Tabatabai connect it to 8:41; Ibn Ashur also relates it to 'We sent down'."}, {"id": "8:42/q01/p2", "position": "An omitted 'remember' governs it.", "reasons": "Wahidi compares 8:26; Zajjaj and Qurtubi paraphrase 'recall when you were there'."}, {"id": "8:42/q01/p3", "position": "The earlier 'met' governs it.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya attaches it to iltaqa in the preceding context."}, {"id": "8:42/q01/p4", "position": "It attaches to al-furqan, the distinction between truth and falsehood.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Samin give this alternative."}, {"id": "8:42/q01/p5", "position": "It attaches to God's attribute qadīr.", "reasons": "Samin, Alusi and Tabatabai reject this because divine power is not confined to that time."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q02", "question": "What does al-ʿudwa mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q02/p1", "position": "The side, lip, or bank of a valley.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan derive it from preventing passage or water crossing; Mawardi places the lip above the bottom and below the top; Layth specifies firm bank ground. Ibn al-Sikkit, Tabarsi and Nahhas give plurals ʿudan, ʿudiyy or ʿudā; Biqai explores related root senses. Poems using ʿadatanī and ʿaddatnī attest restraint."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q03", "question": "How does bi-l-ʿudwa function grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q03/p1", "position": "The prepositional phrase is the predicate of an omitted locative; bi means 'in'.", "reasons": "Samin compares 'Zayd in Mecca'."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q04", "question": "How is al-ʿudwa read?", "turns_on": "Readers and lexicographers differ on the vowel and whether the third form is a dialect or a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q04/p1", "position": "With ḍamma on the ʿayn, an established dialectal reading.", "reasons": "Most Medinan and Kufan readers or the canonical readers besides Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr are cited; some also count Yaqub with the kasra group. Ahmad ibn Yahya, Abu Ubayd and Thaʿlab call ḍamma more common; Aws's line is cited, while Abu Amr and Akhfash dispute its Arabic attestation. Samin rejects denying a mass transmitted form."}, {"id": "8:42/q04/p2", "position": "With kasra on the ʿayn, an established dialectal reading.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr are recurrently named, sometimes Yaqub and other readers. Al-Akhfash says he heard only kasra; al-Yazidi calls it Hijazi. Al-Raʿi and Aws lines attest it. Samin rejects denying either mass transmitted form."}, {"id": "8:42/q04/p3", "position": "With fatḥa on the ʿayn, a third dialect or a place noun formed from a verbal noun.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni cites Qatada, Hasan and Amr; Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi cite additional readers. The form parallels vowel variants in raghwa and other nouns."}, {"id": "8:42/q04/p4", "position": "As al-ʿadiyya, with wāw changed to yāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Samin explain the change after kasra despite the intervening still consonant; analogies include ṣibya, qinya and dunyā."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q05", "question": "Where was the nearer bank, and who occupied it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q05/p1", "position": "The Muslims occupied Badr's bank nearer Medina.", "reasons": "The bank is also described as the northern or upper side; Ibn Atiyya locates Badr between Mecca and Medina and discusses its eastward valley. Wahidi's 'people of meaning' say the nearness to home steadied courage. Jishumi's isolated 'nearer Mecca' differs."}, {"id": "8:42/q05/p2", "position": "The near bank means nearer Mecca.", "reasons": "Jishumi explicitly locates dunyā toward Mecca."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q06", "question": "What is the form and sense of dunyā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q06/p1", "position": "It is the feminine of adnā and means nearer.", "reasons": "The yāʾ replaces root wāw for ease or by the usual feminine pattern; Jishumi also notes the sense 'first life'."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q07", "question": "Who occupied the far bank, and where was it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q07/p1", "position": "The Meccan polytheists occupied the farther bank toward Mecca, away from Medina.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it was a dune and the terms near and far do not rank military quality; Ibn Atiyya gives local geography. Some reports call the enemy lower in the valley."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q08", "question": "Why does quṣwā retain wāw, and how else is it said?", "turns_on": "Morphologists give opposite general rules for nouns and adjectives, but agree the yāʾ form is analogical and the wāw form common.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q08/p1", "position": "Quṣwā is feminine of aqṣā, 'farthest'; quṣyā or qaṣiyā is the analogical alternative.", "reasons": "Hijaz retains wāw and Tamim uses yāʾ. Khalil and Ibn al-Sikkit call retained wāw irregular under the usual change, yet Samin notes it is widely transmitted. Kashshaf likens it to qawd; Alusi links retention to its adjective status. Zayd ibn Ali reads the yāʾ form."}, {"id": "8:42/q08/p2", "position": "Under a reversed morphological rule, adjectives normally change wāw to yāʾ and nouns retain it.", "reasons": "Samin cites ḥazwā in poetry and says this account too makes quṣwā analogically irregular, though common in usage; Alusi reports some morphologists who hold it."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q09", "question": "How do variant wordings describe the two banks?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q09/p1", "position": "Ibn Masʿud's wording calls them the upper and lower banks.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan transmit ʿulyā and suflā."}]}

{"id": "8:42/q12", "question": "What does rakb mean as an Arabic collective?", "turns_on": "Sources differ over whether it is a collective noun or broken plural, and over a numerical threshold.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q12/p1", "position": "A collective noun for riders, especially riders on camels.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Sikkit and Ibn Faris exclude horse riders; Ibn Atiyya says it can pluralize like ṣāḥib/ṣuḥb and is not a very large group. Samin cites diminutive rukayb as proof it is a singular collective, rejecting Akhfash's plural analysis."}, {"id": "8:42/q12/p2", "position": "It denotes at least ten or about ten riders.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports Ibn al-Sikkit; Ibn Atiyya rejects al-Qutaybi's threshold, citing the Prophet's use for three people."}, {"id": "8:42/q12/p3", "position": "It is a broken plural of rider.", "reasons": "Samin reports and rejects al-Akhfash's analysis on the evidence of diminutive rukayb."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q13", "question": "How is 'asfala minkum' parsed and read?", "turns_on": "The normal accusative may be locative, whereas a nominative or comparative analysis makes 'lower' predicative.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q13/p1", "position": "Accusative locative adverb or implied 'in a lower place', functioning as predicate.", "reasons": "Farra, Akhfash, Zajjaj, Sibawayh, Abu Hatim, Kashshaf, Samin, Alusi and Ibn Ashur discuss the omitted place and predicate. Safala contrasts with rising; the caravan lay toward the coast."}, {"id": "8:42/q13/p2", "position": "Nominative 'lower/farther below', sometimes with an implied 'place of the caravan'.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Kisai and Farra permit the comparative or nominative; Zayd ibn Ali reads it nominative. Samin prefers the adverb analysis; Farra contrasts more steeply below."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q14", "question": "How do the clauses about the three groups connect?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q14/p1", "position": "Both wāw clauses coordinate with the opening 'you', dividing the groups' positions.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin call this the better analysis; Alusi also gives coordination."}, {"id": "8:42/q14/p2", "position": "Both wāw clauses are circumstantial, with asfal predicated of the caravan.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin allow this; Alusi says most take the caravan clause as circumstantial to the preceding locative."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q15", "question": "What happened to bring the armies and caravan to Badr?", "turns_on": "Accounts differ over exactly when the parties became aware of one another.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q15/p1", "position": "The Muslims sought Abu Sufyan's caravan; Quraysh moved to protect it; the armies met without an agreed appointment.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq, Ka'b and others report the aims. Ibn Kathir recounts scouts Basbas and Adi, Abu Sufyan's detection of Yathrib date pits and coastal escape, Abu Jahl's refusal to turn back, the return of Banu Zuhra and Banu Adi, captured water carriers, the Prophet's interrogation and prayer, and Sa'd's proposed shelter. Biqai reports Abu Jahl's proud resolve; Islahi mentions a dream and God-guided simultaneous arrival."}, {"id": "8:42/q15/p2", "position": "Mujahid and Umayr say the groups were unaware until the water parties met at Badr.", "reasons": "The Muslims then fought, prevailed and captured Quraysh; Umayr names Abu Jahl's force. Ibn Atiyya objects that the full battle account shows some prior awareness."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q16", "question": "What does the hypothetical failure to keep an appointment mean?", "turns_on": "Explanations turn on fear of relative forces, ordinary timing failures, obstacles, distrust, or the force of the hypothetical itself.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q16/p1", "position": "The Muslims would shrink from facing Quraysh after learning the imbalance.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Ishaq cite fewer Muslims versus numerous enemy. Zamakhshari adds Meccan fear of the Prophet and believers. Alusi rejects this uniform pronoun reading, and Ibn Ashur objects that fear predicts nonattendance rather than different arrival times."}, {"id": "8:42/q16/p2", "position": "They would differ unintentionally in exact timing or place.", "reasons": "Mawardi mentions advance, delay, increase or decrease; Abu Sulayman says the camps would not coincide. Ibn Ashur argues approximate daytime appointments could not reliably bring both armies together at once; timely arrival determined battle prospects according to Islahi."}, {"id": "8:42/q16/p3", "position": "Obstacles and contingencies would prevent the arranged meeting without divine facilitation.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Mawardi, Mahdawi and Tabarsi give impediments. Ibn Atiyya rejects mere obstacles and emphasizes God's facilitation; Abu Hayyan reports Ibn Atiyya as preferring the Mahdawi explanation, a transmission at odds with Ibn Atiyya's own note. Ibn Ashur calls contingencies closest yet incomplete."}, {"id": "8:42/q16/p4", "position": "God alone could bring this meeting about despite human plans and effort.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya stresses divine favor and power, Qushayri recoil, and Tabatabai special will. Al-Kirmani adds Quraysh's distrust and possible ruse; Biqai cites distance and misaligned pace and a possible avoidance like Badr al-Mawʿid; Kuranyolu fears negotiated timing could hurt the Muslims."}, {"id": "8:42/q16/p5", "position": "The counterfactual underscores that arrivals coincided even though planning would probably yield unequal times.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls this the Suhaybiyya law: the result holds even under the imagined condition; he compares 8:23, 6:111, 35:14 and 6:28 and cites Tufayl. Al-Aswad's elegy is a distinct 'as if appointed' comparison. He rejects fear based explanations as mistaking timing for absence."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q17", "question": "Who is meant by 'you' in the meeting conditional?", "turns_on": "Alusi restricts the second pronoun to Muslims, whereas Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur include both armies.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q17/p1", "position": "Both armies are included in both pronouns.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari cites fear on both sides; Ibn Ashur explains grammatical predominance of the addressees; Alusi rejects Zamakhshari's uniform reference as unsuitable."}, {"id": "8:42/q17/p2", "position": "The first pronoun includes both armies, but the second points to the Muslims.", "reasons": "Alusi says the shift fits the stress on Muslim weakness and divine aid."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q18", "question": "What grammatical force does the conditional have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q18/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial, elliptical counterfactual about an arranged battle.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur relates it to the two armies' meeting; Asad expands the implied words, and says commentators accept the ellipsis."}, {"id": "8:42/q18/p2", "position": "Its apodosis can stay true even when its condition is merely imagined.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls this the Suhaybiyya use of law and cites other Quranic cases and Tufayl's poem."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q19", "question": "What is the matter God brought about?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q19/p1", "position": "The divinely decreed Badr victory: Islam and its people raised, idolatry and its people humbled.", "reasons": "Tabari specifies killing and capture, Thalabi and Ibn Ishaq vengeance and favor, Ibn Abbas the promised joy, and Ibn Ashur a great rather than ordinary matter. Damghani and Itqan define qaḍāʾ as carrying out an earlier decree; Tabarsi says manifesting it."}, {"id": "8:42/q19/p2", "position": "God's eternal decree unfolds in time and reveals prior knowledge and assigned destinies.", "reasons": "Sulami quotes Ja'far and others; Qushayri and Ibn Atiyya stress divine decree over planning. Asad says a decree necessarily occurs."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q20", "question": "What does 'was accomplished' mean?", "turns_on": "Kāna can mark an eternally settled matter or its later arrival in actuality.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q20/p1", "position": "It was eternally decreed, certain and bound to happen.", "reasons": "Tabarsi calls it inevitable; Abu Hayyan calls it actual and certain; Alusi appeals to promise in 30:47 or eternal decree; Ibn Ashur says the passive participle treats the future as done and compares 19:21 and 30:47."}, {"id": "8:42/q20/p2", "position": "Kāna can mean ṣāra, 'became accomplished'.", "reasons": "Samin and Alusi report a transition from what had not happened to what then occurred."}]}

{"id": "8:42/q23", "question": "How does the lām in liyahlika connect syntactically?", "turns_on": "Grammarians analyze it as repeated purpose, apposition, attachment to the participle or verb, or conjunction after ellipsis.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q23/p1", "position": "It repeats the first purpose lām, making the second clause an appositive explanation.", "reasons": "Tabari, Nahhas, Thalabi, Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Kashshaf, Razi and Ibn Ashur say the second purpose explains the first; Ibn Ashur says without the lām the verb would be nominative."}, {"id": "8:42/q23/p2", "position": "It attaches to mafʿūlan, stating the completed matter's purpose.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi give this alternative."}, {"id": "8:42/q23/p3", "position": "It attaches directly to yaqḍī.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa gives it; Alusi approves this first option."}, {"id": "8:42/q23/p4", "position": "It coordinates with liyaqḍiya after an omitted conjunction.", "reasons": "Samin calls deletion of the conjunction very rare; Abu Hayyan also lists it."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q24", "question": "How is liyahlika read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q24/p1", "position": "The common form has kasra on lām.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya contrasts it with Aʿmash's fatḥa reading; Alusi gives the ordinary past halaka with present kasra."}, {"id": "8:42/q24/p2", "position": "Al-Aʿmash and others read with fatḥa on lām; a report adds ḍamma on yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan name ʿIsma from Abu Bakr from Asim; Samin cites parallels 4:176 and 40:34; Ibn Jawzi records Khalaf from Yahya. Alusi reports Ibn Jinni objecting on a guttural consonant rule, while al-Qamus admits enabling forms."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q25", "question": "What do perishing and living refer to?", "turns_on": "Death and life may be literal, faith states, communal power, imminent destinies, or an allusion in a later report.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q25/p1", "position": "Disbelief or misguidance and faith or guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq, Qatada, Zajjaj and many later authors take the words metaphorically; Badr removes excuses and makes continued denial obstinate. Ibn Kathir compares 6:122. Ibn Ashur prefers figurative language because survivors were already alive, but specifies communal decline and rise separately."}, {"id": "8:42/q25/p2", "position": "People killed at Badr died, while survivors remained alive, after seeing proof.", "reasons": "Tabari, Thalabi, Mawardi, Abu Hayyan and Asad take literal death and survival. Asad prefers this and adds martyrs' awareness, survivors' recognition of divine victory and opponents' recognition of defeat; Ibn Ashur objects that surviving people were alive already."}, {"id": "8:42/q25/p3", "position": "The defeated community loses strength, while the victorious community rises.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur treats the contrast as communal life and perishing, comparing 9:42, 36:70 and 6:122; Badr exposed support and abandonment."}, {"id": "8:42/q25/p4", "position": "Those approaching, or eternally destined for, death or life are described by their outcome.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi report this temporal or decree based construal; Alusi says life means persistence after the battle."}, {"id": "8:42/q25/p5", "position": "In Aisha's slander report, those who perished are speakers of falsehood about her.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites her account of slander and calumny."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q26", "question": "What is the 'clear proof' at Badr?", "turns_on": "Notes identify the proof as the battle's miraculous outcome, earlier signs or prophetic message, the victory promise, or rain.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q26/p1", "position": "The unexpected victory of a smaller, weaker Muslim army made truth and falsehood plain.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Razi, Biqai, Wahidi and Study Quran cite disparity in numbers and ground; Ibn Ashur says the outcome left no excuse and obliged gratitude. Kuranyolu sees unmistakable support for the right path."}, {"id": "8:42/q26/p2", "position": "Established prophetic signs, miracles and the messenger's warning leave no excuse.", "reasons": "Tabari says witnesses saw a lesson; Thalabi, Baghawi and Wahidi invoke 17:15, no punishment before a messenger. Ibn Ashur emphasizes the visible result."}, {"id": "8:42/q26/p4", "position": "The prebattle rain reversing the ground advantage was the clear proof.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes this reading to some; it compares 8:11."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q27", "question": "What does bayyina mean and apply to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q27/p1", "position": "A clear case or established proof; the prepositional phrase applies to both perishing and living.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls bayyina an adjective; Samin says ʿan bayyina attaches to both verbs."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q28", "question": "What does ʿan mean here?", "turns_on": "It can mark aftermath or derivation, separation, or the sense 'on/against'.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q28/p1", "position": "After or arising from clear proof.", "reasons": "Alusi cites 54:26; Ibn Ashur calls it figurative emergence after evidence clarifies causes. Islahi notes a preposition can mark a source or origin."}, {"id": "8:42/q28/p2", "position": "Separation from, or on/against, clear proof.", "reasons": "Alusi says the Basran separation sense can remain, or it can mean on or against as in 9:34 and Dhū al-Aṣbaʿ's poem."}]}
{"id": "8:42/q29", "question": "How is ḥayya or ḥayiya read and justified?", "turns_on": "The two-yāʾ form preserves the root and analogy, while assimilation treats a fixed-vowel yāʾ like a strong doubled consonant.", "positions": [{"id": "8:42/q29/p1", "position": "The two yāʾs are separately pronounced, ḥayiya.", "reasons": "Reports vary by transmissions: Nafiʿ, Abu Bakr, Bazzī, Yaʿqub and Khalaf are cited.
